title: Ng Giap Hon v. Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd and Others
summary: The Singapore Court of Appeal declined to imply the proposed general good-faith duty into an agency agreement, while distinguishing that issue from narrower terms implied from a particular bargain.
notes:
The supplement’s editorial note at page 73 reports later Canadian and English developments, including Wastech, Braganza, and Yam Seng. Those are later editorial comparisons, not holdings of the 2009 Singapore court. No current status of those jurisdictions is asserted here.

The decision is Ng Giap Hon v Westcomb Securities Pte Ltd [2009] SGCA 19; Ng was a remisier claiming commission on IPO placement shares allocated to two of the firm's customers, and the Court of Appeal declined to imply a duty of good faith as a matter of law, citing the sanctity of contract and the uncertainty such a duty would create in future cases.

sections.Parties: Ng Giap Hon was a remisier, a self-employed securities intermediary affiliated with a brokerage. Westcomb Securities was the contracting broker; related companies and others were also respondents in the underlying dispute.
sections.Material Facts:
The 2005 agency agreement appointed Ng as the broker’s agent and entitled him to a percentage of commissions charged on transactions dealt by or through him. It expressly denied an employment relationship and contained an entire-agreement clause. Ng introduced prospective investors and helped arrange account-opening discussions. He alleged that forms and transactions were redirected away from him and that IPO purchases proceeded without commissions, depriving him of earnings.

The trial judge found that the brokerage had no express or implied obligation to charge commissions on IPO placements, which were often allocated to favored clients without commission. On appeal Ng proposed two implied terms: a general duty of good faith between principal and agent, and a specific obligation not to deprive him of commission.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court rejected the contractual, custom, conspiracy, and quantum-meruit claims described by the editors. On appeal Ng abandoned quantum meruit, and the Court of Appeal accepted the trial court’s treatment of conspiracy and alleged customary commission practice. The assigned excerpt reports that the entire-agreement clause did not bar implication of terms, then reproduces the rejection of the general good-faith term. It does not reproduce the final analysis of the narrower term or the formal disposition of the entire appeal.
sections.Issue: Could a general duty of good faith be implied by law into this agency agreement, and how did that question differ from implying a term in fact?
sections.Holding: The proposed general good-faith term should not be implied by law into this agreement on the reasoning reproduced. The entire-agreement clause was not itself a categorical bar to implied terms. The remaining, narrower implied-term issue is not resolved in the supplied extract.
sections.Reasoning:
A term implied in fact fills a gap by reference to what the particular contracting parties would have intended. A term implied in law imposes a rule for a category of contracts on broader policy grounds. The latter choice has precedential consequences beyond the particular parties and requires separate justification.

The court emphasized the unsettled meaning and application of a general good-faith doctrine in the jurisdictions it surveyed in 2009. It reviewed Summers’ approach of identifying forms of bad faith, Burton’s account of recapturing opportunities surrendered by contract, and arguments that ordinary interpretation and implication already address the relevant misconduct. It considered the conceptual disagreement a substantial reason for caution about adopting the general term proposed. This reasoning does not establish that dishonest conduct is always lawful or that a specific contractual restraint on commission diversion could never be implied.

textbookImport.scope: Assigned edited supplemental excerpt; narrower implied-term analysis and final appellate disposition omitted

learning.why: Ng Giap belongs beside Dalton and Market Street as a jurisdiction-specific counterpoint. It also explains why the source and specificity of a proposed limit on discretion matter.

topics.discretion: Tests a proposed limit on a broker’s choices about charging and allocating commissions.
topics.good-faith: Rejects the proposed general implied duty in the 2009 Singapore setting.
topics.interpretation: Separates terms implied in fact from terms implied in law.
topics.governing-law: Demonstrates jurisdictional variation in good-faith doctrine.
topics.gap-filling: The opinion turns on the distinction between terms implied in law across a class of contracts and terms implied in fact from a particular bargain.
topics.integration: The court held that an entire-agreement clause does not by itself bar the implication of terms.

mnemonic.rationale: IPO shares and a remisier’s commission
